investigations.name: two-species-community
investigations.description:
A single glucose/acetate pool is shared by two E. coli core genome-scale models with no spatial separation. Each species is its own CRMProcess -> FBAStep pair: a Monod consumer-resource layer sets per-resource uptake targets from the current pool, and dynamic FBA turns those targets into exchange bounds, solves for growth, and writes realized substrate deltas back to the shared pool. Because both FBA steps read and write the same substrates store, one species' overflow becomes the other's feedstock.

The glucose specialist has high glucose Vmax, low acetate Vmax, and a tight oxygen cap (EX_o2_e lower = -6). Under that O2 limitation the LP cannot fully oxidize its glucose influx and secretes acetate as overflow — a Crabtree-like phenotype. The acetate specialist has low glucose affinity and high acetate Vmax, so it grows poorly on glucose but well on the acetate the first species leaks. The prediction is niche partitioning: an early glucose-driven bloom of the first species that builds an acetate pool, followed by a later acetate-driven bloom of the second.

The study runs the composite from a 15 mM glucose / 0 mM acetate pool with a 4:1 initial biomass split favouring the glucose specialist, records per-species biomass and the two shared pools, and checks three behaviours: glucose is drawn to zero, the acetate pool shows a transient overflow peak, and the acetate specialist does the majority of its growth after that peak.
investigations.title: Two-species cross-feeding community
investigations.objective: When a glucose specialist and an acetate specialist share a single glucose/acetate pool with no spatial separation, does CRM-constrained dynamic FBA reproduce niche differentiation by cross-feeding — i.e. does the glucose specialist's acetate overflow sustain distinct, temporally offset growth of the acetate specialist — rather than simple competitive exclusion?
investigations.claim: The glucose specialist's acetate overflow sustains a distinct acetate specialist: 93% of the acetate specialist's biomass gain occurs after the acetate pool peaks, and glucose is exhausted exactly at the peak (t=8.3) — niche differentiation by cross-feeding, not competitive exclusion.
